However, they lack a building inventory that characterizes the makeup of housing units, their occupants, and their energy consumption to inform those decisions. To address these issues, representatives from PBC OOR and NREL’s E2C Expert Match team agreed on a scope of work to characterize the existing residential building stock through four tasks. The first task was to use publicly available data from the NREL’s ResStockTM model to characterize the following attributes of PBC’s residential building stock: building type, renter/owner status, size (square footage), age of buildings (vintage), HVAC system types, and, for multi-family buildings, number of units. The second task was to compare ResStock data to existing local open-source data provided by the client to validate the ResStock data and add any additional perspective to the residential building stock characterization in the first task. The third task was to complete an analysis of ResStock data to quantify the potential changes in energy demand, utility costs, and greenhouse gas emissions from the baseline residential building stock in PBC compared to 16 upgrade packages. The outcomes from each of these tasks are outlined in the sections that follow. Task 1: Residential building stock characterization using ResStock What is ResStock? ResStock is a physics-based, bottom-up, white box, residential building stock energy model developed by NREL.6 Figure 1 gives an overview of the three-part workflow for the ResStock model. First, a residential building stock is generated using the data from several national-level surveys and other data sources.7 Next, the sub-hourly energy use of each housing unit in the building stock is calculated using its building characteristics, local weather data, and occupant behavior. Additionally, upgrade measures can be applied to any housing unit and the same calculation of sub-hourly energy use will be performed with these upgrades applied. In this way, it is possible to attribute the change in energy consumption in each simulated housing unit to the specific upgrade measures applied to that housing unit. Last, high-performance computing resources summarize this sub-hourly data into annual energy consumption, utility bill, and emissions data for the entire building stock modeled. This data can be used to inform decisions about building retrofitting measures that can be made to the building stock to achieve the varying levels of energy, utility bill, or emissions impact.
